The dabakan is a single-headed membranophone from the Philippines, H-S number 211.261.2, and in the kulintang ensemble it takes the supporting part; it is also the only non-gong element among the five main instruments of the Maguindanao ensemble. The body is usually hourglass-, cone-, tube- or goblet-shaped, hollowed from coconut or jackfruit wood, and the head is goatskin, buffalo hide, deerskin, snakeskin or lizard skin, fixed with metal wire and rattan hoops. Players usually stand, holding two rattan or bamboo sticks and striking the head with the wrist, and the sound is short and muffled, with damping, rolls and open strokes. It is used to keep the speed of the ensemble, and it can accompany the kutiyapi, or in the Maranao Kasorondayong (a way of playing) two players face each other and interlock rhythms.
達巴幹鼓為膜鳴樂器，單面鼓皮，以藤或竹製鼓棒敲擊鼓面，聲音多為短促而悶，可借鼓棒: The dabakan is a membranophone with a single head; it is struck with rattan or bamboo sticks and the sound is mostly short and muffled, with damping, rolls and open strokes coming from the spring of the stick. Changes of volume and timbre depend mainly on where the stick lands and on damping, and striking the side of the body or the rim of the opening gives other rhythmic colours.
